column1: # Traduzione inglese dei testi del corso Tongji (lezioni 11-19, prima parte).

column2: How much are the grapes per jin?
A 还是 B? (alternative question)
To offer a choice between two possibilities use 还是; the sentence doesn’t take 吗.
Do you drink tea or coffee?
以前 and 以后
On their own: “before / in the past” and “after / in the future”. After a verb or a time word: …以前 = before…, …以后 = after…
I used to like coffee.
Since I came to China I’ve got used to drinking tea.
Adjective + 一点儿
After an adjective or a verb, 一点儿 means “a bit (more)”: 便宜一点儿 = a bit cheaper.
It’s too expensive, make it a bit cheaper.
At the fruit stall
Are these mandarins sweet?
Very sweet. You can try them.
Delicious! How much per jin?
Five yuan.
Could you make it a bit cheaper?
Let’s say 4.50. How many jin would you like?
I’ll take two jin. And a jin of grapes too.
That’s fifteen yuan altogether.
Yamada’s tastes

Yamada is Japanese. He used to like coffee; since he came to China he has got used to drinking tea. He also likes Chinese food, especially dumplings. He says the canteen dumplings are delicious and cheap, and he can even finish half a jin of them.
The white sun sets behind the mountains, the Yellow River flows into the sea. If you want to see a thousand li further, climb one more floor of the tower.
They say that at the entrance of sixty-six alleys lives old Liu, sixty-six years old. (For l / n and the tones of liù)
What are you doing?
Actions in progress, moods, chatting and inviting someone in
有点儿 + adjective / verb
“A bit”, almost always for something unpleasant or negative: 有点儿累, 有点儿贵, 有点儿想家. (Not to be confused with 一点儿, which goes after the adjective.)
I’m a bit down today.
I’m a bit homesick.
咱们 and 我们
咱们 always includes the listener (“we, you and I”); 我们 can also exclude them (“we, but not you”).
Let’s have a chat, you and me.
We have class tomorrow, and you?
着: a lasting state
Verb + 着 describes a continuing state: 门开着 = the door is open. V1 + 着 + V2: you do V2 while V1 goes on.
The door is open, come on in.
He does his homework listening to music.
呢: action in progress
Verb + object + 呢 (or 在 + verb + 呢) shows an action in progress: “I’m doing”.
What are you doing? — I’m doing my homework.
“Really?”: shows surprise or a little doubt.
There’s no class tomorrow. — Really?
好像 and 觉得
好像 = “it seems (that)”, an outside impression; 觉得 = “I feel, I think”, a personal opinion.
You seem a bit down.
I don’t think this habit is very good.
In front of Yamada’s room
Yamada, what are you doing?
I’m writing characters, there’s a dictation tomorrow.
There are too many characters! I’m a bit anxious.
Let’s have a chat.
Gladly! Come in, the door is open.
Do you write characters while listening to music?
Of course! I think it works.
Sunday in the dorm

On Sunday morning everyone is in the dorm. Yamada is listening to music with the door open; Peter is writing characters because there’s a dictation tomorrow; Annie and Lisa are chatting. And what is Jeff doing? He’s still asleep!

Beans are cooked by burning their own stalks; in the pot the beans weep: “We grew from the same root, why such haste to torment us?” (Legend says Cao Zhi composed it in seven steps, on the orders of his brother the emperor.)
A toothbrush can brush teeth, to brush your teeth you use a toothbrush. (For sh / s)
I’m going to the library to borrow books
The library, buying online, sending and receiving parcels
“If… then…”: 要是 introduces the condition, 就 (before the verb) the consequence.
If you don’t understand, ask the teacher.
If I have time tomorrow, I’ll go to the library.
不过 and 可是
Both mean “but, however”. 不过 is softer and often just adds a remark; 可是 marks a stronger contrast.
This book is excellent, but it’s a bit expensive.
Verb + 到
到 after the verb shows that the action reaches its goal (借到 = to manage to borrow) or arrives somewhere (送到宿舍, 寄到上海). Negative: 没(有) + V + 到.
I didn’t manage to borrow that book.
The parcel was delivered to my dorm.
就: sooner than expected
就 before the verb stresses that the action happens early or easily (the opposite of 才).
I was already up at eight.
The book arrived as early as this morning.
Verb + 一下
Makes the action brief or the request more polite: 填一下, 看一下, 等一下.
Please fill in this form.
“And / with”: links nouns and pronouns, not whole sentences. 和……一起 = together with…
I’ll come with you.
Buying a book online
Piao Zhiyong
Liu Wei, I want to buy an English book: the library doesn’t have it.
Liu Wei
Buy it online: it’s convenient and not expensive.
But I don’t know how to do it.
No problem, I’ll help you place the order.
Can the book be delivered to the dorm?
Yes. If you order today, it arrives tomorrow.
Great! How do I pay?
You pay with your phone, it’s really easy.
A super-fast parcel

Yesterday afternoon Yamada bought a phone online. This morning the courier has already delivered it to his dorm. The courier says: “Have a quick look: if everything is fine, write your name here.” Yamada checks: the phone is perfect. He says: “That was so fast! Thank you!”
山居秋暝 · 王维 (first verse)
On the empty mountain, after the fresh rain, the evening air feels like autumn. The bright moon shines through the pines, the clear spring flows over the stones.
What’s the weather like today?
Weather and seasons; asking about health and studies; sending news home
…怎么样？ (weather, health, studies)
With 怎么样 you ask what a situation is like: 天气怎么样? 身体怎么样? 学习怎么样?
How have you been lately?
Expressing degree
From highest to lowest: 非常好 · 很好 · 不错 · 还可以 · 不太好 · 不好. 不错 is a positive judgement, 还可以 means “so-so, OK”.
The weather is nice today.
The canteen food is OK.
Surname + 阿姨 is used for a woman of your parents’ age (a family friend, a neighbour). It is affectionate and respectful.
Hello, Auntie Wang!
听说 + sentence
“I’ve heard that…”: reports information received from others.
I heard you were ill: are you better now?
让 + person + verb
“To make / let someone do…”. 请告诉 + person + message = “please tell… that…”.
Tell my mother not to worry.
The weather: 下雨
To rain = 下雨 (下小雨 = to drizzle). For wind say 风很大 / 有风.
It drizzled last night.
It’s very windy here in winter.
“Already”: the action or change has happened.
I’ve already recovered.
On the phone with Auntie Wang
Auntie Wang
Zhang Xin, what’s the weather like where you are?
Zhang Xin
It’s autumn now, the weather is lovely: neither cold nor hot.
I’ve heard summers there are extremely hot.
Yes, in summer it’s hot and it often rains.
Have you been busy studying lately?
A bit, but I’m very well.
And the canteen food?
There are lots of dishes and they’re cheap. Auntie, please tell mum not to worry.
The seasons according to Jeff

I’m English and I study Chinese in China. Here spring is neither cold nor hot, but it’s very windy. Summer is very hot, even at night. In autumn the weather is especially nice: I really love autumn. Winter is freezing: I need to buy a coat.
Over a thousand mountains the birds have vanished, on ten thousand paths the footprints are gone. In a lonely boat, an old man in a straw cape and hat fishes alone in the snow on the frozen river.
How many classes are there in a week?
School calendar, duration, past experiences, ordinal numbers and holidays
过: experience
Verb + 过 = to have done something at least once in your life (or in the past). Negative: 没(有) + V + 过. Question: V过…吗? / V过…没有?
I’ve been to the Great Wall.
I’ve never had Peking duck.
The teacher said so: winter holidays are in January.
多 + adjective: how…?
多长时间? = how long? 多大? = how old? After a round number, 多 means “and more”: 一个多月 = over a month.
How long are the winter holidays? — Over a month.
一月 and 一个月
一月 is the name of the month (January); 一个月 is a length of time (one month). Likewise: 星期一 (Monday) / 一个星期 (one week).
The winter holidays start in January and last a month.
Duration after the verb
The duration goes after the verb: V (+ 了) + duration (+ object).
I studied Chinese for six months.
We had ten days of holiday.
第 + number: ordinals
第一 (first), 第二次 (the second time), 第三周 (the third week).
It’s the first time I’ve come to China.
每 + (number +) measure word + noun, often with 都 before the verb: “every…”.
I have class every day.
太……了 = too; 只 = only; …的时候 = when…
There are too many students in our class.
We often chat while we eat.
Before the end of the semester
Lisa, when are the end-of-semester exams?
The teacher told us: on 10 January.
How many exams are there?
Three: grammar, spoken Chinese and listening.
Do the holidays start right after the exams?
Yes, and they last over a month. Are you going home?
No. I haven’t been to the Great Wall yet: I want to go and see Beijing.
I’ve been there twice. And Peking duck in Beijing is delicious!
Peter’s week

This semester Peter has five subjects: grammar, spoken Chinese, listening, characters and calligraphy. He has 22 class hours a week: from Monday to Friday he has four every morning, and on Tuesday and Thursday afternoons there is calligraphy as well. There are fifteen students in his class. Peter says: “It’s quite a lot of classes, but I really like them.”
赋得古原草送别 · 白居易 (first verse)
Lush grass on the plain: every year it withers and flourishes again. The prairie fire cannot burn it all: when the spring wind blows, it grows back.
Dates and addresses

In Chinese you always go from big to small. Dates: 2025年10月9号 (year, month, day). Addresses: country, city, district, street or university, building, room (中国上海市……大学3号楼502房间). On envelopes, after the recipient’s name you write 收 (“to receive”).
Excuse me, how do I get to the zoo?
Asking for and giving directions, forms of address, floors of a building
Forms of address
To address someone: 先生 (sir), 同学 (to a student), 大夫 (to a doctor), 阿姨 (to a woman of your parents’ age). They go at the start of the sentence.
Excuse me, sir, where is the bank?
Doctor, I have toothache.
To ask the way: 去 + place + 怎么走? To answer: 往 + direction + 走 / 拐 (to turn).
Excuse me, how do you get to the zoo?
Go straight on and turn right at the crossroads.
Place + 就是
就是 stresses “right there / that’s exactly it”.
The bank is right there on the left side of the road.
Duration + 就到了
走几分钟就到了 = “it’s just a few minutes’ walk”: 就 shows that little is needed.
It’s a five-minute walk.
A warm thank-you (“thank you so much!”). The reply is 不客气 / 不用谢.
Thank you so much! — You’re welcome.
Floors: 层 / 楼
二层 or 二楼 = the second floor (in China the ground floor is 一层). 上楼 = to go upstairs.
The dentist is on the second floor: go on up.
再 (again / then)
再 + verb: to repeat the action or to do it later.
Try asking someone else.
On the street
Excuse me, sir, how do I get to the bank?
Passer-by
Is it far?
No, it’s a five-minute walk. The bank is next to the bookshop.
On the left or the right side of the road?
The left.
Thank you so much!
You’re welcome.
Yamada looks for a dictionary

Yamada wants to buy a dictionary. He asks a classmate: “Where do they sell dictionaries?” The classmate answers: “There’s a bookshop west of the school: go straight on and turn left at the crossroads, it’s there.” After a ten-minute walk Yamada arrives. The bookshop has three floors and the dictionaries are on the second. Yamada goes upstairs and buys a Chinese-English dictionary.
Under the pines I ask the young disciple; he says his master has gone to gather herbs. “He is somewhere on this mountain, but the clouds are thick and I don’t know where.”
Tasty and cheap
At the restaurant: ordering, flavours, quantities, the bill; making comparisons
Joins two qualities that go together, both positive or both negative.
The dishes here are tasty and cheap.
I like sweet and sour dishes.
At the end of a list: “and so on, etc.”.
In the canteen there are dumplings, noodles, rice and so on.
来 + quantity + dish
At a restaurant 来 means “bring / I’ll have…”.
We’ll have tomato and egg and two bowls of rice.
The potential complement
V + 得 + result = to manage; V + 不 + result = not to manage: 吃得完 / 吃不完 (can / can’t finish eating), 看得懂 / 看不懂, 说不清楚.
There are too many dishes, we can’t finish them.
I can’t really describe this flavour.
Comparisons with 比
A 比 B + adjective. To say “much more” add 多了, for “a bit” 一点儿. With 比 you don’t use 很 / 非常.
Dumplings are tastier than noodles.
Today is a bit colder than yesterday.
别 + verb
A prohibition or negative advice: “don’t…!”.
Don’t worry, this dish isn’t spicy.
会 + verb = to know how to do something (because you learned it); it can also mean that something will probably happen.
I can make dumplings.
Will it rain tomorrow?
Polite measure word for people: 几位? = how many of you?
Welcome! How many of you are there?
At the restaurant
Waiter
Welcome! Two of you?
Yes, two.
Here’s the menu. What would you like?
Zhang Xin, what do you want to eat?
I don’t eat spicy food. Let’s have tomato and egg.
OK. And a sweet and sour fish and a soup.
Would you like rice?
Two bowls. Are the dishes enough?
That’s enough. They say the food here is good and cheap!
Just a moment, the dishes are coming right away.
The little restaurant near school

(Annie tells us) Next to our school there’s a small restaurant where the food is good and cheap. I really like their dumplings: they’re much better than the canteen ones. Last week I went there with Lisa: we ordered three dishes and two bowls of noodles, and we only spent sixty yuan altogether. There was too much food, we couldn’t finish it and had the leftovers packed to take away.

Hoeing the grain under the midday sun, sweat drips onto the soil beneath the seedlings. Who knows that, in the bowl, every grain is the fruit of hard work? (Chinese children learn it so as not to waste food.)
Eating together

In a Chinese restaurant dishes are ordered for the whole table and shared; usually you order about one dish per person plus a soup, and rice is ordered separately. To call the waiter you say out loud 服务员!; asking to 打包 the leftovers is perfectly normal.
Will you be my tutor?
Asking for help with studying, agreeing on times, describing how something is done
行 = “OK, fine”. 那不行 is a firm refusal: “no way, out of the question”.
Will you tutor me for an hour a day, OK? — OK.
You don’t want money? Out of the question!
Introduces a suggestion or a compromise: “let’s do this”.
Let’s do this: we’ll meet on Wednesday.
Adjective + 地 + verb
地 turns the adjective into an adverb of manner, before the verb: 认真地练习 (to practise conscientiously).
She practises her tones conscientiously.
He says happily: “Great!”
The complement of degree with 得
V + 得 + adjective describes how an action is done: 说得很好. With an object the verb is repeated: (V) + O + V + 得 + adjective. Question: V得怎么样?
You speak Chinese very well!
How does he sing? — Quite well.
“Quite, rather” (spoken).
This method is quite good.
从 + time + 开始 = starting from; 互相 + verb = each other; 一定 = definitely.
Starting next week I’ll practise for an hour a day.
Let’s help each other practise speaking.
I’ll definitely be there!
Asking for help
Wenjing, I’d like to ask you a favour.
Li Wenjing
What is it? Go ahead.
My handwriting is bad: can you tutor me?
Sure. How many times a week?
Three times, half an hour each time: OK?
OK. Let’s do this: Monday, Wednesday and Friday at seven in the evening, in the library.
Great! Which day do we start?
From next Monday.
Thank you! I promise I’ll practise hard.
Peter’s tutor

Li Wenjing is Peter’s tutor. She tutors him quite well and is always very conscientious. They practise writing characters and chat about life in France and in China: Peter finds it very interesting. Now Peter writes characters much better than before. He hopes to have Wenjing as his tutor next semester too.
The man is at rest, osmanthus flowers fall; the night is still, the spring mountain empty. The moon rises and startles the mountain birds, which now and then sing in the spring stream.
I don’t feel very well
Health and symptoms, at the doctor’s, an exam gone badly, worrying about someone, saying goodbye
有点儿 and 一点儿
有点儿 goes BEFORE the adjective and points to something unpleasant: 有点儿不舒服. 一点儿 goes AFTER the adjective, for comparisons or requests: 好一点儿了, 快一点儿.
I have a slight fever.
I feel a bit better than yesterday.
好好儿 + reduplicated verb
好好儿 = properly, as you should; it is often combined with a reduplicated verb to give friendly advice.
Before the exam you must revise properly.
“It doesn’t matter, never mind”: a reply to an apology or a way to comfort someone.
Sorry! — Never mind.
The exam went badly? Never mind, prepare well next time.
没 and 没有
Both negate 有 and past actions. As a short answer only 没有 is used.
Have you revised? — No.
